why.Stehekin and the Park Creek trail: When the lake boat and High Bridge shuttle schedule fits, this skips the long Thunder Creek walk and reaches the Park Creek trail with the least distance on foot.
why.Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin vall: When the boat and shuttle cannot be made to work, a party can drive to the west-side road end, walk over Cascade Pass and down the valley, at the cost of extra miles and a pass climb.

review.notes: Thunder Creek is the long, commonly cited approach; Stehekin and Cascade Pass are the alternates (Cascade Pass about 5.5 miles longer than the Stehekin start).

why.Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT s: To trade a few miles of switchbacks for a brushy, windfall-strewn cut across the hillside; for parties who would rather thrash than walk the longer trail.

review.notes: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks is the documented standard; the Lemah Creek and Meadows line is an alternate that joins the PCT. Reason for the shortcut rests partly on stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks

why.The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Por: For parties starting from the Bacon Creek road side who want to skip the Ross Lake crossing and Big Beaver trail, accepting a long, pathless ridge route with no tread to follow.

review.notes: Big Beaver and Access Creek is well documented as the usual way in; found nothing detailed on the southern Bacon Creek line, so the reason is cautious and partly from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass

why.Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side: For a gentler grade from a higher trailhead, or to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side, at the price of a creek ford.

review.notes: Both approaches are documented, with Foggy Dew via Merchants Basin the stored primary; no source ranks them head to head, so the reason leans on stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side

why.Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' pat: Once the snow has gone, from about July, when the couloir is a loose scree slog and the boot path is visible, though the gullies are brushier.

review.notes: Reports agree the classic season is late spring on snow, later it becomes loose scree; both ways use the same Lena Lake approach, so the marked primary is defensible as a season choice.

problems: Both ways in are the same Lena Lake approach and differ only by season; they are not really alternative approaches, and the summer way (which describes the path itself) is the one not marked Most used.

why.Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, lef: When the lake outlet is hard to cross, or to avoid a ford altogether, at the cost of a slide-alder bushwhack and a longer, steeper climb up the gully.

review.notes: Outlet line takes about an hour from the lake; the Aasgard gully line takes 1.5-2 hours and is also described as an established option.

why.Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental: Once snow buries the summer trail, when the usual talus slopes become avalanche paths and the party travels the valley floor toward Source Lake instead.

review.notes: Reports confirm the summer path is avoided in winter because of avalanche danger near Source Lake.

why.Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road d: Only if the road is ever repaired and open to vehicles again, when driving to the trailhead turns the trip from an overnight walk or bike ride into a shorter outing.

review.notes: Reports say the forest road is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge and is walked or biked, so the closure variation is what parties actually do.

problems: The two ways in are not alternatives: the walk-or-bike-the-road variation and the trailhead trail are one trip. The trailhead way's name still says road drivable, which current reports contradict.

why.Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT: Starts higher for an open, easy walk along the Pacific Crest Trail, and suits a through-trip that exits by Surprise Creek, at the cost of extra mileage.

review.notes: Both reach Trap Pass; sources disagree on which is shorter, so the reason is cautious.
Trip reports for the couloir are spring ski and snow trips from the Cascade Pass side; the valley approach has little documentation, so its reason leans on stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below

problems: why withdrawn in review: it described a snowless couloir as the reason, which contradicts the climb

why.Up the valley from the landing, then off: Midsummer, when the basin is walkable, for parties who would rather ride the ferry and shuttle than cross and recross the pass, accepting a longer, unmarked valley push.

review.notes: Little online coverage; the pass-from-the-river-road way is consistent with trip reports reaching the lake from the Cascade Pass side. The reason comes from stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin

why.Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier: Early in the season, or for parties camping in the north-side basin, since it avoids the long Ingalls and Goat Pass hike; leaves the car opposite the usual descent.

review.notes: Reports describe the southern Ingalls and Goat Pass approach as the usual one for the upper ridge, with the Mountaineer Creek approach as the north-side alternative.
